segments.text: Hey everyone, I'm Sarah Lean and welcome
to this video. Today we're diving into
something that's super important if
you're working with Terraform,
understanding the Terraform state file
and how it deals with state drift using
the refresh only flag. So let's get into
it. Terraform relies on a state file.
This file acts as the single source of
truth for the infrastructure you've
deployed. It maps the real world
infrastructure to your Terraform
configuration. By keeping this state,
Terraform can figure out what's changed,
what needs to be changed, and
importantly, what doesn't. This helps it
avoid recreating things
unnecessarily. But what happens when
changes are made outside of Terraform?
Maybe someone's used the Azure portal,
PowerShell, or a CLI to tweak a
resource. That's what we call state
drift. State drift is when your actual
infrastructure doesn't match what
Terraform thinks is there. And that
mismatch, it can lead to some really
unexpected behavior next time you try to
apply changes with Terraform. If you're
enjoying this content or finding it
helpful, don't forget to hit that like
button and subscribe to the channel. It
really helps support the content I
create and helps you stay in the loop
with all things infrastructure and
automation. To handle drift, Terraform
lets us refresh the state file, checking
what's really out there and updating it
accordingly. In older versions, this was
done with Terraform refresh, but that's
now deprecated. Instead, with version
0.15.4 onwards, we use the refresh only
flag with either the plan or apply
commands. So, here's how it works. First
make sure Terraform is initialized using
Terraform in it. Then check the current
state versus real world infrastructure
with Terraform
plan-refresh dash
only. This gives you a clear difference
between what Terraform thinks exists and
what's actually deployed. It's a safe
way to preview the drift before doing
anything else. And finally, when you're
happy with what's being updated, run
Terraform
apply-refresh-only. That will update
your Terraform state without making
actual infrastructure changes, just
bringing the state back in sync with
everything. Now, this fits perfectly
with Terraform's plan and apply model.
review first, then act, minimizing
surprises and improving control,
especially when you're working in teams
or using CI/CD pipelines. Now, a few
best practices that I personally follow
when using the refresh only. Always run
Terraform plan refresh only before any
apply. It gives you that early warning
of
drift. Review all changes before
applying. Don't just assume that they
may be small or they might be important.
Communicate in team environment so
everyone's on the same page before that
state file gets updated. So there you
have it. Refresh only is a really
powerful way to keep your Terraform stay
accurate and avoid nasty surprises when
you're managing your
infrastructure. Now, if you found this
video useful, please hit that like
